newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major gets tough on EU, Blair scornful.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major gets tough on EU, Blair scornful.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major threatened to defy Europe once again on Tuesday over a deal on fish catches as polls showed his election campaign appearing to lose momentum.
His campaign rival, Labour leader Tony Blair, derided the government's handling of the fish row, saying Mickey Mouse could have won a better deal for Britain.

But, dashing hopes in Brussels that a Blair victory in the May 1 poll could herald a new era of cooperation between Britain and its EU partners, Blair said he would have told a Labour minister to vote against Tuesday's deal on fish quotas.
"I certainly would have done that," Blair said in an interview with Sky television news, underlining the harder line against Europe the Labour leader has adopted as the campaign has progressed.
Major, like Blair on the campaign trail, said earlier that Britain would not accept the EU plan to cut fishing quotas by 30 percent until Brussels solved the problem of so-called "quota hoppers"

"I have not a shred of intention of cutting the British catch until or unless we get a satisfactory agreement on quota hopping," Major told reporters during a campaign visit to the town of Tavistock in western England.

Quota hopping refers to the perfectly legal practice whereby foreign fishermen, mainly Spanish and Dutch, have bought up about 25 percent of the British fishing fleet to gain greater access to EU catch quotas.
Britain, backed only by France, was outvoted when EU fisheries ministers meeting in Luxembourg on Tuesday decided on the 30 percent cuts in catches in a move designed to preserve fish stocks.
Blair, visiting the south coast resort of Brighton, compared the row to Major's handling of the beef crisis in the wake of the scare over mad cow disease.
A European export ban is still in place despite Major's decision to block a European summit in Italy last year until what he called a timetable to end the ban was agreed.

Blair said after a question and answer session with university students: "A Labour government will get a better deal for the British fishing industry. In my view Mickey Mouse would get a better deal than this lot."

Conservative strategists hoped the new row, already being dubbed a "fish war" by Britain's media, would bolster the party's image as tough on Europe -- an image they believe appeals to their core voters.

But Labour strategists were delighted the spotlight remained on Europe after news that a Conservative party vice-chairwoman, Angela Rumbold, was defying Major's "wait-and-see" policy on the single European currency.
Rumbold, head of the party's candidates' department, said in an election address to her south London constituents that she would under no circumstances vote to give up the pound sterling.

Blair seized on the address as a sign of a divided and weak leadership unable to control his own party, adding that if re-elected, the Conservatives would tear themselves apart "like ferrets in a sack" over Europe.
The Conservatives have responded by intensifying the personal attacks on Blair, accusing him of hypocrisy over education policy and describing his leadership style as dictatorial.

A Gallup poll for Wednesday's Daily Telegraph showed a 21 point lead for Labour, three points more than before the weekend and the same lead as a MORI poll for the Evening Standard newspaper on Tuesday.
The polls appeared to rule out a dip in Labour support claimed by Conservative aides last week after two polls showed a narrowing of Blair's lead.
